_note: NOVA tips (situations) and facts (shown on quiet turns). Numbers are approximate teaching values. Sources marked TODO: verify still need a checked NASA URL.

items.text: Mission Planning: pick where you fly and how hard. The Moon is close and forgiving; Mars is the long game.
Personnel: your seat decides which calls are yours. Teammates cover the rest, so pick people whose strengths fill your gaps.
The Briefing table is the planning board. Every part costs mass, power and money from one shared pot.
Launch Control: everyone votes go or no-go. One real no-go stops the launch.
Moon: about 3 days away, and you can talk to Earth almost live. Watch out for the two-week lunar night.
Mars: months away, and messages take minutes. Your crew will lean on standing orders.
Over mass or budget. Lighter parts, fewer spares or a bigger rocket: each fix costs something else.
A supply is under 30 %. Check the Power & Life Support panel for the days left.
Power problem: batteries carry you only so long. Shedding science load buys time.
Comms problem: science only counts once it reaches Earth. A stuck backlog is a quiet loss.
Crew problem: tired or upset people make more mistakes. Rest is a real repair.
The environment bites back: dust, radiation and flares. Shelter and spares are your friends.
The repair failed. Try again with a rested crew member, or do it yourself at the station.
Hands-on task: finish it in time and the odds go up. The clock only runs while the panel is open.
Under signal delay, urgent problems are handled by your standing orders before you can answer.
Lunar night: two weeks without sun. Batteries and fuel cells keep the heaters and air running.
Good science day! Data only counts once it is sent home, so keep the downlink clear.
Go / no-go: warnings can be accepted, failures cannot. Read every seat before you launch.
Debrief: every red line has a cause. Fix the biggest one and fly again.
A day on the Moon, sunrise to sunrise, lasts about 29.5 Earth days: roughly two weeks of light, then two weeks of night.
A radio message between Earth and Mars takes roughly 4 to 24 minutes one way, depending on where the planets are.
Mars dust is fine enough to coat solar panels. Some rovers lost much of their power to it; others were saved by gusts of wind.
Every breath adds CO2 to the cabin air. Scrubbers pull it out; without them the air would turn unsafe within hours.
The Moon and Mars have no global magnetic field like Earth, so their surfaces get far more space radiation.
Most of a rocket is fuel. Every extra kilogram of payload needs more fuel to lift it, so mass drives cost.
